title: Floods, Droughts and Landslides in India

cards.h: The hazards that hit India every year
cards.b: Floods, droughts and landslides cause the most frequent losses in India. They are linked to monsoon variation, relief and human activity. UPSC asks for causes, vulnerable areas, mitigation and the policy framework. This lesson adds depth to the general hazard overview.

Heavy rain, river silt, embankment breaches, glacial lake bursts, cyclone storm surge, and urban drains clogged by encroachment. About 40 million hectares, roughly an eighth of the land, is flood-prone, per the Rashtriya Barh Ayog (1980). Brahmaputra, Ganga and Kosi plains see the worst riverine floods; Assam floods nearly every year.

Floods: Assam and the northeast (Brahmaputra, Barak), Bihar (Kosi, Gandak, Bagmati), Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal (Damodar), Odisha delta rivers, Andhra and Telangana (Godavari, Krishna). Urban floods: Mumbai 2005 (944 mm in a day), Chennai 2015, Srinagar 2014, Kerala 2018 and 2019, Hyderabad 2020, Bengaluru 2022.

Structural: dams, embankments, channel improvement, flood walls. Non-structural: forecasting (Central Water Commission), flood plain zoning, early warning, insurance, and the Flood Management and Border Areas Programme. Embankments can raise riverbeds and trap silt, so some experts prefer room for the river. Urban drainage and wetland protection matter.

IMD defines a drought year when seasonal rain is less than 90 percent of the long period average (in the all-India case, deficiency over 10 percent). Types: meteorological (rain deficit), hydrological (low rivers and groundwater), agricultural (soil moisture and crop loss). About 16 percent of the country is drought-prone, mostly in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra (Marathwada, Vidarbha), Karnataka, Andhra (Rayalaseema), Telangana and Odisha.

Drought Management Guidelines (2010, NDMA), MGNREGA wage work, crop insurance (PMFBY), watershed development, the Jal Shakti Abhiyan and Atal Bhujal Yojana. The Manual for Drought Management (2016, revised 2020) sets triggers. Years of national drought: 1965-66, 1972, 1987, 2002, 2009, 2014-15. Cause linked to El Nino and weak monsoon.

Slope failure caused by steep slopes, weak and fractured rock, heavy rain, earthquakes and human cuts for roads and buildings. India has about 12 percent of its land at risk. Hotspots: the Himalaya (Uttarakhand, Himachal, Sikkim), the northeast, the Western Ghats (Kerala, Karnataka, Goa) and the Nilgiris. The Geological Survey of India (GSI) leads mapping and the National Landslide Susceptibility Map.

Malin, Maharashtra (2014), Kedarnath (2013), Kerala's Kavalappara and Puthumala (2019), Wayanad (July 2024), Joshimath subsidence (2023). Mitigation: avoid building on unstable slopes, retaining walls, drainage, afforestation, geotextiles, early warning systems and rainfall thresholds. The NDMA Landslide guidelines (2009) and the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy (2019) guide policy.

Disaster Management Act 2005: NDMA, SDMA, DDMA. NDRF (2006), SDRF, the 15th Finance Commission's allocation to the National and State Disaster Mitigation Funds. The shift is from relief-centric to prevention, led by the Sendai Framework (2015-30). Kerala's State plans after 2018 and Odisha's cyclone model are models.

Likely questions: 'Why does Assam face floods every year?', 'Differentiate types of drought', 'Landslides in the Himalaya: causes and mitigation'.

  • Split into natural and anthropogenic causes.
  • Split measures into structural and non-structural.
  • Quote one institution and one scheme.
